messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame was seven years old the first time his father came home with that particular heat on his skin—the dry, oppressive warmth of a room left closed all day in a Lagos compound, the air thick and still. He remembered the way his father’s hand felt, rough and hot against his cheek, and then the floor, and then the sound of footsteps pacing afterward, circling, never stopping. That was the texture that stayed with him: not the pain itself, but the sensation of that heat, and the grit of a concrete floor against his palm, and the rhythm of footsteps that meant someone was still there, still angry, still deciding what came next. By the time he was ten, Kwame had learned to read those footsteps from three rooms away—a quickening pace meant danger, a slow drag meant exhaustion, and either way his body would go cold and still, waiting. He never told anyone. He learned to keep his face empty and his voice flat, and when he left Nigeria at nineteen for the United States, he believed he had left that room behind.

Now, at twenty-seven, Kwame drove a taxi in Chicago, and the city had a thousand ways of bringing him back. It was the feel of a passenger’s sleeve brushing his arm in the backseat—a certain synthetic fabric that made his stomach drop before he even knew why. It was the blast of heat from a car’s heater on a cold night, hitting his face just so, and suddenly his hands would be shaking on the wheel. And it was the footsteps. On the street, in a parking garage, behind him at a gas station—the sound of someone walking at a certain pace, close enough to catch up—and Kwame would feel his throat close and his pulse hammer, and he would know, with absolute certainty, that he was not safe. His body kept reacting as if it were still that room, as if the danger were still present, and he had come to believe that his body was an enemy, a traitor that refused to learn that the past was over. He was certain he had permanently changed for the worse—that the boy who might have trusted people, who might have felt at home anywhere, had been replaced by someone who flinched at a stranger’s coat.

When the triggers hit, Kwame did what he had to do. He would crank the window down, even in winter, to change the temperature on his skin. He would turn the radio up loud—loud enough to drown out footsteps, loud enough to fill his head with noise so there was no room for the memory. He had started smoking marijuana in the evenings to take the edge off, telling himself it was just to sleep, but lately he was smoking before his shift too, just to get through the first few fares. And he avoided intimacy. He had not been on a date in two years, and when a passenger tried to make conversation—asked where he was from, how long he had been driving—he would give short answers and keep his eyes on the road. Being close to anyone meant being vulnerable, and being vulnerable meant being caught off guard, and being caught off guard meant the footsteps could find him. The more he avoided, the more he felt cut off from the world. He had lost his connection to his community—he no longer called his cousins in Lagos, no longer visited the Ghanaian church on the South Side where he used to feel a kind of belonging. He told himself they would not understand, that he was too different now, that the person they remembered was gone.

The hypervigilance was constant. He scanned every rearview mirror, every sidewalk, every shadow between parked cars. He took risks he knew were reckless—driving through red lights at empty intersections just to keep moving, picking up fares in neighborhoods other drivers avoided, because a part of him felt that if he could survive danger on his own terms, it would not catch him by surprise. But the vigilance also made the triggers worse. The more he watched for footsteps, the more he heard them. The more he braced for the texture of a passenger’s coat, the more his skin seemed to remember it. And every time his body reacted—every time his hands shook or his breath went shallow—he felt the belief harden: he was broken, he was unsafe, he would never feel at home in his own skin.

What finally brought Kwame to a therapist’s office was a single moment. A passenger, a middle-aged woman, had touched his shoulder to thank him for a smooth ride, and the warmth of her hand through his jacket had sent him into a full panic. He had pulled over, asked her to get out, and sat shaking in the driver’s seat for twenty minutes. That night, he could not stop thinking about how small his life had become—how the room he had escaped as a child had followed him across an ocean and built itself inside his chest. He came to therapy because he was tired of being afraid, and because he was terrified that if he did not change something, he would spend the rest of his life driving through a city he could not trust, listening for footsteps that were never there.
